newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia projects large drop in economic growth.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia projects large drop in economic growth.

text.p: Cambodia's projected gross domestic product (GDP) growth for 1997 has been slashed to three percent in the wake of bloody fighting in the capital last month, a top finance official said on Monday.
Undersecretary of State for Finance Chea Peng Chheng told Reuters GDP growth had previously been forecast at six to seven percent.

"We are concerned about economic growth in Cambodia," he told Reuters. "I believe we cannot get the (six to seven percent) figure because of an economic slowdown and inflation... The situation in Cambodia is affecting investment."
"I believe that GDP for 1997 will drop to three percent," he said.
Year-on-year inflation for July surged to 16.55 percent compared with 7.34 percent in June, according to a Ministry of Finance report released on Monday.
Month-on-month inflation for July was 12.97 percent, up from 0.64 percent in June and 0.67 percent in May.

"The inflation is up because of the serious clashes in Phnom Penh, the drop in the riel and lack of imports in the wake of the fighting," Kim Phalla, deputy director of the Economic Unit of the Ministry of Finance, told Reuters.
The Cambodian riel has depreciated to just over 3,000 to the dollar from 2,800 before the fighting in early July, officials said.
"The economy is in trouble," said an Asian diplomat.
"Investors who were already here have to stay, but new ones aren't coming. They see instability and deals being unilaterally cancelled."
The diplomat cited the cancellation of flag carrier Royal Air Cambodge's monopoly over domestic air service and the closure of the Taipei trade office by Second Prime Minister Hun Sen last month.
"People aren't expanding their investment here unless they're already committed," said Craig Martin, manager of International Management and Investment Consultants Ltd.
"The macro-economic future is that of a slower growth rate and increased inflation," he said.
Hun Sen ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh on July 6 after two days of fighting in the capital and a subsequent day of looting that caused about $50 million in damage to businesses.
Cambodia's GDP growth of six to 6.5 percent last year was largely driven by foreign investment and foreign aid, the latter accounting for nearly half of the national budget, officials said.
The coup has scared away some foreign investment and the United States and Germany have frozen aid to Cambodia in response to Hun Sen's power grab, they said.

"The problem is concerning the modern economy, which is driven by foreign aid and investment. That is what the economy depends on, and there are too many uncertainties there," said a Cambodian economic adviser to the Finance Ministry.
Government revenues are also down, though statistics are not yet available, officials said. A finance ministry official predicted July revenues had dropped 20 percent from targeted levels.
"The government relies very heavily on customs duties, and if retail sales and (imports)... are down, that's going to directly affect the revenue of the government," Martin said.
